option1: Directly construct and call all four classes (PaymentValidator, FraudCheckService, PaymentGateway, NotificationService) itself, in the correct order, every single time it needs to process an order
option2: The caller would need to extend all four classes simultaneously
option3: The order would fail to process without a facade, since Java enforces facades at the compiler level
option4: Nothing changes — Java requires a facade class to call any other class
correctOptionExplanation: Without a facade, every caller has to independently know about and correctly sequence all four subsystem classes themselves.

questionText: What's the single concrete thing checkout(Order order) actually saves a caller from having to know?
option2: The specific four classes involved, and the specific order they must be called in
option3: How to write a for loop
option4: Nothing — checkout() doesn't actually save anything, it's purely cosmetic
correctOptionExplanation: The facade's value is hiding both which classes are involved and the correct sequence to call them in.

questionText: If NotificationService.sendReceipt() were accidentally called BEFORE PaymentGateway.charge() inside checkout(), what would happen?
option1: It would cause a compile error, since Java enforces call order automatically
option2: PaymentGateway.charge() would silently be skipped instead
option3: A receipt would be sent for a payment that hasn't actually been charged yet — a real ordering bug, since checkout()'s whole value is calling these four steps in the CORRECT sequence
option4: Nothing — the four calls are independent of each other and order never matters
correctOptionExplanation: Sequencing correctness is entirely the programmer's responsibility inside checkout() — nothing in Java enforces the right order automatically.

questionText: Given the previous answer, restate precisely what CheckoutFacade is actually guaranteeing to every caller.
option1: That no exceptions can ever be thrown during checkout
option2: That the four subsystem classes will never change their own internal logic
option3: That Order objects are immutable once constructed
option4: That the four subsystem calls always happen in the one correct sequence, every single time, regardless of which part of the app is calling checkout() — removing the risk of any caller getting the order wrong themselves
correctOptionExplanation: This is the facade's actual guarantee: consistent, correct sequencing, centralized in one place instead of duplicated and potentially mis-ordered across callers.

questionText: CheckoutFacade does NOT implement any shared interface with PaymentValidator, FraudCheckService, PaymentGateway, or NotificationService — there's no common ICheckout interface any of them satisfy. How does this differ from PaymentDecorator (which DOES implements IPayment, the same interface Card/UPI implement)?
option1: CheckoutFacade isn't standing in for or substituting any single one of the four classes — it's coordinating four unrelated classes into a new, higher-level operation, whereas PaymentDecorator specifically pretends to BE an IPayment, substitutable anywhere an IPayment is expected
option2: CheckoutFacade actually does implement a shared interface, it's just not shown in this code
option3: There's no real difference — both are just wrapping classes with identical design rules
option4: PaymentDecorator also coordinates four unrelated classes, identical to CheckoutFacade
correctOptionExplanation: Facade coordinates multiple unrelated classes into a new operation; Decorator substitutes for one specific interface it shares with what it wraps — genuinely different jobs.

questionText: Given the previous answer, is CheckoutFacade substitutable anywhere PaymentValidator is expected (the way FeeDecorator is substitutable anywhere IPayment is expected)?
option1: Yes — any wrapping class is automatically substitutable for whatever it wraps
option2: No — CheckoutFacade implements no shared interface with any of the four classes it wraps, so it cannot be passed anywhere a PaymentValidator, FraudCheckService, PaymentGateway, or NotificationService specifically is expected
option3: This can't be determined without seeing Order's code
option4: Yes, but only for PaymentGateway specifically
correctOptionExplanation: Substitutability requires a shared interface, which CheckoutFacade deliberately doesn't have with any of its four wrapped classes.

questionText: A new team member says: "Since CheckoutFacade isn't required to implement any interface and doesn't need to satisfy any type-substitutability rule, is it fair to say Facade has basically no structural design constraint compared to something like Adapter?" Is this a fair characterization?
option1: No — Facade actually has the exact same interface-implementation requirement as Adapter
option2: Yes, but only because CheckoutFacade happens to be badly written; a "correct" Facade would implement an interface
option3: Yes — this is a fair and accurate characterization; Facade's whole mechanism really is just "group several calls into one method, in the right order," with no interface contract, no polymorphism requirement, and no compiler-enforced rule backing it, unlike Adapter (which MUST satisfy a target interface) or Decorator (which MUST remain substitutable for what it wraps)
option4: No — Facade requires at least three wrapped classes to be considered valid
correctOptionExplanation: This is an honest assessment: Facade genuinely lacks the structural mechanism that backs Adapter and Decorator.

questionText: Given the previous honest assessment — that Facade has no real structural mechanism — what's the actual value it provides, if not type-safety or substitutability?
option1: Its only value is reducing the total number of classes in a codebase
option2: It has no real value at all and should never be used
option3: It provides the same compile-time guarantees as Adapter and Decorator, just phrased differently
option4: Organizational/readability value: it designates ONE sanctioned, simple entry point for a multi-step operation, so callers don't need to understand or duplicate the internal coordination logic themselves — the value is about hiding complexity and preventing duplicated, error-prone call sequences, not about any type-system guarantee
correctOptionExplanation: Facade's value is entirely organizational — reducing duplicated coordination knowledge across the codebase, not any compiler-enforced guarantee.

questionText: CheckoutFacade's constructor directly does this.validator = new PaymentValidator(); (and similarly for the other three). What real testing problem does this specific detail create?
option1: Since the four subsystem objects are constructed directly inside CheckoutFacade's own constructor (not injected from outside), a test cannot substitute fake/test versions of PaymentValidator, FraudCheckService, etc. — unlike Processor(IPayment ip) from the Adapter example, which accepts its dependency externally and is trivially testable with a fake
option2: This only matters if PaymentValidator has a private constructor
option3: There's no testing problem here — CheckoutFacade is exactly as testable as Processor
option4: checkout() cannot be called at all until this is fixed
correctOptionExplanation: Constructing dependencies internally rather than accepting them makes substituting test doubles impossible — a real, common testability cost.

questionText: How would you fix the testing problem from the previous question, using a technique already established earlier in this course (see Processor(IPayment ip), FeeDecorator(IPayment ip, FeeStrategy feeStrategy))?
option2: Change CheckoutFacade's constructor to accept the four dependencies as parameters (public CheckoutFacade(PaymentValidator validator, FraudCheckService fraudCheck, PaymentGateway gateway, NotificationService notifier)) instead of constructing them internally — the same dependency-injection technique used everywhere else in the course, allowing tests to inject fakes for each of the four
option3: There is no way to fix this; CheckoutFacade is fundamentally untestable by design
option4: Make all four fields public static so tests can overwrite them directly
correctOptionExplanation: Constructor injection is the same fix used consistently throughout the course whenever a class needs to be testable with fakes.

questionText: Recall the two soft rules discussed for Facade: dependency should only flow one way (subsystem classes should never know the facade exists), and the facade should coordinate, not accumulate new business logic. Suppose checkout() is later modified to include its own custom fraud-scoring math directly inside CheckoutFacade, rather than delegating that scoring to FraudCheckService. What real problem does this create?
option1: It would make checkout() faster, since fewer classes need to be constructed
option2: It would cause a compile error, since Java forbids logic inside facade methods
option3: The fraud-scoring logic now lives somewhere with no dedicated home, no focused class of its own, and likely no direct unit test coverage — the facade quietly stops being just an orchestrator and starts being a place where real, untested business logic accumulates, which undermines the whole "simple, thin entry point" idea
option4: This is actually the correct way to extend a Facade — accumulating logic directly inside it is expected and encouraged
correctOptionExplanation: Logic creeping into a facade undermines the entire reason it exists: to stay a thin, simple coordination layer.

questionText: Given the previous question, if that fraud-scoring math genuinely needs to live somewhere, what's the correct fix, consistent with keeping CheckoutFacade a thin coordinator?
option1: Delete the fraud-scoring feature entirely, since Facades cannot support new features
option2: Leave the logic inside checkout() permanently, since moving it elsewhere would break the Facade pattern
option3: Turn CheckoutFacade into an abstract class so subclasses can override the scoring logic
option4: Extract the fraud-scoring math into its own properly named class (or back into FraudCheckService itself) with its own tests, and have checkout() simply call it — the same way it calls validator.validate() or gateway.charge() — restoring the facade to pure coordination rather than logic ownership
correctOptionExplanation: The fix is always the same: give new logic its own properly tested home, and have the facade simply call it like everything else.

questionText: Suppose PaymentGateway (one of the four subsystem classes) needed to call back into CheckoutFacade — say, to trigger checkout()'s notification step directly after a successful charge, bypassing the rest of checkout()'s sequence. What design problem does this introduce?
option1: A circular dependency — CheckoutFacade depends on PaymentGateway (it holds a PaymentGateway field), and now PaymentGateway would also depend on CheckoutFacade, which breaks the intended one-directional relationship where subsystem classes stay unaware of whatever coordinates them, and makes both classes harder to reason about, test, or reuse independently
option2: There's no problem — bidirectional dependencies between a facade and its subsystem are the expected, correct design
option3: Circular dependencies are automatically resolved by the Java compiler, so this is a non-issue
option4: This would only be a problem if PaymentGateway were declared final
correctOptionExplanation: One-directional dependency (facade knows subsystem, never the reverse) is one of the two soft rules that keeps a facade coherent.

questionText: A caller decides to bypass CheckoutFacade entirely and call gateway.charge(order.getAmount()) directly, skipping validation, fraud-checking, and notification altogether — maybe for a special internal admin refund flow that genuinely doesn't need those steps. Does the existence of CheckoutFacade prevent this?
option1: Yes, but only if PaymentGateway's constructor is marked private
option2: No — nothing about Facade prevents direct access to the subsystem classes it wraps; unlike Adapter (where the caller genuinely cannot use the incompatible class directly without translation) or a properly encapsulated field (private access), a Facade is a convenience path, not an enforced boundary, so callers remain free to go around it when they have a real reason to
option3: No, but only because this specific example forgot to add access restrictions; a "correct" Facade always blocks direct access
option4: Yes — Facade always makes its wrapped classes private and inaccessible from outside
correctOptionExplanation: Facade offers a convenient default path, not an enforced boundary — direct access to the subsystem always remains possible.

questionText: Given the previous answer — that a Facade doesn't actually block direct access to what it wraps — is this a design flaw in CheckoutFacade, or is it consistent with what Facade is actually meant to be?
option1: It's a flaw specific to Java; other languages enforce this automatically
option2: It can only be fixed by converting CheckoutFacade into a Singleton
option3: It's consistent with the pattern's actual purpose — Facade exists to offer a simpler, safer default path for the common case, not to lock down or forbid access to the underlying subsystem for legitimate edge cases that genuinely need finer control; enforcing hard access restriction was never Facade's job
option4: It's a design flaw; every Facade must make its wrapped classes completely inaccessible to be considered correctly implemented
correctOptionExplanation: Not restricting access is a deliberate, correct property of Facade, not an oversight — it's meant to be a helpful default, not a locked door.

questionText: Pull the whole quiz together: CheckoutFacade has no interface contract, no substitutability guarantee, doesn't block direct access to what it wraps, and can accidentally accumulate untested logic if you're not careful. Given all of that, state the ONE thing Facade genuinely, reliably provides that justifies giving it a name at all.
option1: Automatic dependency injection for every class it wraps
option2: Guaranteed thread-safety across all four wrapped subsystem classes
option3: A guarantee that the wrapped subsystem classes can never be called directly by any other code
option4: A single, deliberately designated entry point that correctly sequences and coordinates several otherwise-scattered subsystem calls, so most callers never need to independently learn, remember, or duplicate that coordination logic themselves — the value is entirely about reducing duplicated coordination knowledge across a codebase, not about any structural or type-safety guarantee
correctOptionExplanation: This is the honest, complete summary of Facade's real value: a single coordination point, nothing more, nothing enforced by the compiler.
